title: Tòmas Odhar's hand on the gatepost
summary: At the fallen gate of the Muileann chrom store the old hewer Tòmas Odhar rests his hand flat on the gatepost and says he has carried coal out through it for six-and-thirty years and never thought to see rifles carried out through it instead. His words are repeated round the camp for a week after.

title: Mòrag takes the sergeant's rifle herself
summary: Mòrag nic Iain Maor lifts the surrendered sergeant's rifle from the cobbles of the Muileann chrom store with her own hand rather than leave it to be gathered by another, the first weapon she has carried since she broke the overseer's staff the summer before.

title: Pàdraig Reamhar scuttles his own barge
summary: The boatman Pàdraig Reamhar, who built the larger of the two barges sunk at Ceann fhada with his own father twenty years before, knocks the plugs from her hull with his own hands and says afterward only that she had been a good boat.

title: Oswin Frayne rowed out from Ceann fhada
summary: A' Chompanaidh's harbour-master at Ceann fhada, Oswin Frayne, is rowed out past his own sunk barges and set aboard a boat for any harbour still flying Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir's flag, unharmed, on the crews' own order.

title: Bread goes to the half-loaf at Baile thais
summary: By the seventh day of the siege of the walled store, the camp at Baile thais cuts its bread to a half-loaf a household, and the children who had at first jeered at the wall grow quiet and keep to their mothers' fires.

title: The constables of Baile thais sent to the coast
summary: On Eilidh nic Raghnaill's written order, carried down from Comhairle na Coille by a girl of fourteen, Seumas Ciar sends the thirty-one constables who yield the Baile thais store to the coast whole and fed, over the objection of hewers who have buried kin to the same walls.

title: The cairn on the moor above Cnoc naomh
summary: Crew-leaders of Baile gharbh and the northern pits leave a cairn of spoil-stones, one from each pit, on the moor above Cnoc naomh the night they fix the week of the rising, and are gone before the shrine's own watcher finds it at dawn.

title: The northern constables walk south
summary: The constables taken at Muileann shean and Tobar ghorm are sent south on foot with no guard at all, and reach Rathad na Mèinne inside two days, talking loudly of how the whole north has gone over in a single week.

title: Uilleam Gobha's first grenades tried
summary: On a moonless night behind his forge at Muileann dhearg, Uilleam Gobha tries the first of his tin-cased grenades, with only his eldest son holding a lamp a safe way off, and says it will do.

title: A finger lost before Uilleam Gobha's care
summary: Before Uilleam Gobha takes up the crimping of the powder tins himself, another smith of Muileann dhearg loses three fingers to the work, a loss Uilleam afterward says he was determined it would not cost him.

title: Aonghas shuts his own gates on Rathad na Mèinne
summary: Aonghas (of An Taigh-seinnse Mòr) shuts the gates of An Taigh-seinnse Mòr across Rathad na Mèinne with his own hands, and the men he has kept in its loft since autumn come down armed, cutting the road at its half-way stage.

title: The council-hall lock broken with a coal-hammer
summary: The custodians of Cathair dhearg break Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir's locks on their own council-hall doors with a coal-hammer borrowed from the smithy across the square, and sit down again in the chairs shut from them for two years.

title: The coal-carts turned on their sides
summary: The townsfolk of Cathair dhearg barricade the coal-cart bridge with A' Chompanaidh's own carts, turned on their sides and lashed together with ironmonger's chain, and hold it three days until the constables sent against it are called back to the harbour.

title: The Cathair dhomhain warehouse left swinging
summary: The townsfolk of Cathair dhomhain carry off the tools, rope and stored powder of A' Chompanaidh's first warehouse and leave it standing empty with its doors swinging, unlocked, for anyone to see.

title: Muileann mhin's boats go down to the capital
summary: After three days of argument turning as much on trade as on loyalty, Muileann mhin sends its boats to the council at Cathair dhearg, and through that winter and the next carries food down the Abhainn fhionn by night.

title: Strake's letter asking for a ship before winter
summary: Lionel Strake writes to A' Chompanaidh's directors over the sea that the harbour town below Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir holds itself apart from the fighting only until it judges which side will leave it better off, and asks for more men, powder and a ship before the northern passage closes.

title: The turnip cart to the ford
summary: A cart with a false floor of turnips carries Uilleam Gobha's grenades up the cut coal road to the crews waiting at the ford of Àth chiar, the first of his work to leave Muileann dhearg for open fighting.

title: The nineteen of Àth chiar buried
summary: The council's clerk Fionnuala writes down by lamp-light the names of the nineteen dead of Àth chiar and reads the list aloud the next morning; within the week they are buried on the moor above Cnoc naomh, within sight of the cairn raised there before the fighting began.
